24VDC Power Supply Sizing for Control Panels: Load List, Margin, Inrush, Derating, Redundancy and Voltage Drop

One undersized 24 V supply can reset a PLC every time a group of coils switches on. Here you add up every load, apply margin and temperature derating, plan redundancy and check the voltage that actually reaches the field.

Load List 22 mA Rule 25% Margin Derating Calculator

Work out the current rating of a 24 V DC supply from the real load list of a PLC or instrument panel. The calculator adds margin and temperature derating, and the solved example shows each step with numbers.

Hello everyone, today we are going to work through 24VDC power supply sizing for a control panel, from the load list and margin to derating, redundancy and field voltage drop.
Quick Answer

What is 24VDC power supply sizing and how do you calculate the rating?

24VDC power supply sizing means adding the steady current of every load on the 24 V bus, adding a 20 to 25 percent margin and correcting for panel temperature. Rating = (sum of loads × 1.25) ÷ derating factor. Example: a 6.65 A load needs 8.31 A with margin, and at 65 °C (factor 0.875) the supply must give 9.50 A, so you pick a 10 A unit.

What Is 24VDC Power Supply Sizing?

24VDC power supply sizing is the job of choosing a DC supply whose rated current covers every load on the 24 V bus, plus margin, at the hottest temperature inside the panel. You size on current, then check inrush, redundancy and the voltage left at the far end of each field cable.

Key Facts
  • IEC 61131 part 2 gives 20.4 to 28.8 V as the operating range for 24 V DC PLC supplies.
  • Allow 22 mA for every 4 to 20 mA loop, because a failed transmitter can drive its signal above 21 mA.
  • Eaton adds 20 percent to the calculated nominal load for longer supply life.
  • Phoenix Contact QUINT units derate output by 2.5 percent per kelvin above 60 °C.

For the background on this voltage, read why PLC systems use 24 volts.

Do You Know?

Eaton sizes a supply on two separate totals: the surge current of all loads and their sealed, steady current. A supply can pass the steady test and still fail when every coil pulls in at the same moment.

How Do You Calculate 24V Power Supply Load?

You calculate the 24 V load by listing every device on the supply, taking its maximum current from the datasheet and adding the currents together. Where a datasheet gives watts, divide by 24 to get amps.

1
PLC and IO
CPU, IO modules and backplane from the PLC power budget.
2
Transmitters
Every two wire loop at 22 mA, not 20 mA.
3
Solenoids
Coil current at 24 V, or watts divided by 24.
4
Relays
Every relay coil that can be energised together.
5
Other loads
HMI, network switch, lamps, fans and field devices.
6
Sum
Add all currents; multiply by 24 for watts.
Load (example panel)QtyCurrent eachTotal
PLC CPU and IO modules1 set2.5 A2.50 A
Two wire transmitters2422 mA0.53 A
Solenoid valve coils80.35 A2.80 A
Interface relays160.02 A0.32 A
HMI, switch and lamps1 lot0.5 A0.50 A
Steady load6.65 A (159.6 W)

The currents in this table are example values, so take the real ones from each datasheet. Module current for a rack is usually listed in the PLC power budget, as covered in IO modules in industrial automation.

A two wire transmitter draws its loop current from the panel supply, so 24 loops at 22 mA add about half an amp. In this example the solenoids are the largest block; the solenoid valve working principle covers how the coil works.

Fit suppression diodes on relay coils as shown in relay coil suppression, so turn off spikes stay off the 24 V bus.

Quick Tip

Count only loads that can be on together, and write that assumption on the load list. If the sequence can energise every solenoid at once, size for all of them.

24VDC Power Supply Sizing Formula and Calculator

In 24VDC power supply sizing, the rating you need is the steady load plus margin, divided by the temperature derating factor. The calculator uses the Phoenix Contact QUINT figure of 2.5 percent per kelvin above 60 °C and picks the next standard size.

Steady load I = PLC + (Ntx × 22 mA) + solenoids + relays + other
With margin = I × (1 + margin ÷ 100)
Derating factor = 1 minus 0.025 × (T minus 60), for T above 60 °C
Required rating = I with margin ÷ derating factor
24 V DC Supply Rating Calculator
Result
Load 6.65 A (159.6 W), with margin 8.31 A, after derating 9.50 A: choose a 10 A (240 W) supply

Solved example: the panel in the load table runs at 65 °C inside, and we want 25 percent margin. Here are the same numbers the calculator uses by default.

I = 2.5 + 0.528 + 2.8 + 0.32 + 0.5 = 6.65 A
With margin = 6.648 × 1.25 = 8.31 A
Derating factor = 1 minus 0.025 × 5 = 0.875
Required = 8.31 ÷ 0.875 = 9.50 A
Choose a 10 A, 240 W supply

At 50 °C the same panel would need only 8.31 A. For the transmitter side of the same panel, check each loop with our HART loop voltage budget calculator.

How Much Margin Should a 24V Power Supply Have?

Keep 20 to 25 percent margin over the calculated steady load. Eaton uses 20 percent for extended life, and the RSP Supply sizing guide warns against picking a supply whose rating only equals the total load.

Margin also covers loops added during commissioning, and a cooler supply ages more slowly, as covered in power supply aging in automation.

Right margin (20 to 25%)
  • Covers spare IO and later devices
  • Supply runs cooler and lasts longer
  • Short overloads stay in boost range
Wrong margin
  • None: supply trips on start up
  • Too much: cost, heat and rail space
  • Added twice by two engineers
Design Tip
Write the margin and the ambient temperature on the load list itself. The next engineer who adds loops can then see how much spare current is left.

Why Does Inrush Current Trip a 24V Supply?

Inrush trips a supply when the surge of many loads starting together is higher than the short time current the supply can deliver. Coils, PLC module input capacitors and HMI start up all add to it.

Power onAll module capacitors charge at once.
Coils pull inContactor and relay coils draw pull in current.
Supply limitCurrent exceeds the boost range.
ResultVoltage dips, CPU resets or supply hiccups.

Eaton sums the inrush of each coil and checks the total against the supply surge rating, which for its PSG range is a 1 second surge at 10 second intervals.

The Phoenix Contact QUINT4 40 A datasheet gives a static boost of 45 A, a dynamic boost of 60 A for 5 seconds and 215 A for 15 ms to trip a branch fuse. Size the branch protection with the fuse selection guide and MCB rating method, so that a shorted field cable opens its own fuse.

Do You Know?

The QUINT4 datasheet says its 215 A fuse breaking pulse is about 6 times nominal current. It is meant to blow a small branch fuse quickly.

How Does Ambient Temperature Derate a Power Supply?

Above a stated temperature, the supply must deliver less current to stay inside its limits. For Phoenix Contact QUINT supplies and their redundancy modules, output falls by 2.5 percent per kelvin above 60 °C, up to 70 °C.

Use the air temperature near the supply, which is often higher than the room. Estimate it with the panel heat load calculation, since the losses of the supply itself are part of that heat.

Quick Tip

Put the supply low in the panel, away from drives and braking resistors. The ambient you enter in the calculator should be the hottest summer value, not the commissioning day reading.

How to Build a Redundant 24 V Supply With Diode or ORing Modules

For redundancy you run two supplies in parallel through a diode or MOSFET ORing module, and each supply must carry the whole load alone. Phoenix Contact states this rule in the QUINT DIODE datasheet, so that if one unit fails the other takes over without a break.

Diode module

QUINT DIODE drops 0.5 V and loses up to 10 W at 20 A.

Best for: Simple N+1 panels
Low cost
MOSFET ORing

QUINT ORING drops 0.2 V at 40 A with up to 8 W loss.

Best for: High current buses
Low loss
Separate buses

One supply for system loads, another for solenoids.

Best for: Noisy field loads
Isolation

The diode drop comes off the bus, so set the supply output a little higher; the QUINT4 adjusts from 24 to 29.5 V. See Schottky diode limitations and full layouts in redundant power supply for PLC.

Myth: Two 5 A supplies in parallel give a redundant 10 A supply.
Fact: Each supply must carry the full load alone, so a 10 A load needs two 10 A units.
Myth: Any diode can be used to parallel two supplies.
Fact: The diode must carry full current; QUINT DIODE loses up to 10 W at 20 A.
Myth: Redundant supplies remove the need for branch fuses.
Fact: A shorted field cable still pulls the bus down unless its fuse opens.

How Do You Check Voltage Drop to Field Instruments?

Multiply the loop length by two, by the current and by the cable resistance per metre, and subtract the result from the supply voltage. The device at the far end must still see a voltage above its minimum supply rating.

V drop = 2 × L × I × R ÷ 1000
L = one way length (m), R = ohm per km
Example: 2 × 200 × 0.35 × 12.1 ÷ 1000 = 1.69 V
Coil voltage = 24.0 minus 1.69 = 22.3 V

The 12.1 ohm per km figure is the IEC 60228 maximum for 1.5 mm² copper at 20 °C, and hot cable has a higher resistance. Pick the core size with cable size for load current, or work it out online with this cable voltage drop calculator.

Transmitter loops share voltage between cable, the PLC analog input resistor and the transmitter. See cable sizing basics for how resistance grows with length.

Field symptomLikely causeWhat to check
CPU resets when coils switch onSupply too small for inrushSurge total vs boost rating
Far solenoid drops outCable voltage dropCoil voltage under load
Supply trips on hot daysNo temperature deratingPanel ambient
One redundant unit takes all loadUnequal output settingsSet both outputs equal
Quick Tip

Measure the voltage at the device terminals with the load running. A reading taken at the supply terminals hides the cable drop.

24VDC Power Supply Sizing Checklist

Run through this checklist before you freeze the supply on the panel drawing.

  • Every 24 V load listed with its datasheet current
  • Transmitters counted at 22 mA each
  • Margin of 20 to 25 percent added once
  • Derating applied for the hottest panel ambient
  • Each redundant supply sized for the full load
  • Voltage at the farthest device checked under load

Keep system power and field power on separate fused branches, as shown in PLC wiring from field instrument to system cabinet and marshalling cabinet wiring. A short in one field cable then stays in its own branch.

24VDC Power Supply Sizing FAQ

What is 24VDC power supply sizing in a PLC control panel?

24VDC power supply sizing is selecting a DC supply whose current rating covers all panel and field loads with margin. For a 6.65 A load with 25 percent margin you need at least 8.31 A, before any derating for temperature.

How to calculate 24V power supply current step by step with example?

List every load, add the currents, multiply by 1.25 and divide by the derating factor. A 6.65 A load at 65 °C gives 6.65 × 1.25 ÷ 0.875 = 9.50 A.

Then choose the next standard size, here 10 A.

Why should each 4 to 20 mA transmitter be counted at 22 mA?

A failed transmitter can drive its signal above 21 mA under NAMUR NE43, so 20 mA is too low for sizing. Counting 22 mA per loop covers that alarm current with a little room, and 24 loops then add 0.53 A to the panel load.

What is the difference between steady load current and inrush current?

Steady load is the current loads draw once running, while inrush is the short surge at switch on. Eaton sums both separately for every coil, and the supply surge rating must cover the inrush total even when the steady load fits easily.

How does temperature derating change the required power supply rating?

Above 60 °C, Phoenix Contact QUINT supplies lose 2.5 percent of output per kelvin. At 65 °C the factor is 0.875, so an 8.31 A requirement grows to 9.50 A, and a supply sized at room temperature can trip on a hot day.

What is a common mistake when sizing redundant 24 V power supplies?

The usual mistake is sharing the load across two units so that neither can carry it alone. Phoenix Contact states that each redundant supply must handle the full load, so a 10 A load needs two 10 A supplies and a suitable diode or ORing module.

Which cable size keeps voltage drop low for 24 V field solenoids?

Choose a size where the drop at full coil current leaves the device above its minimum voltage. A 0.35 A coil at 200 m on 1.5 mm² copper drops 1.69 V, so longer runs or bigger coils may need 2.5 mm² cable.

What We Learn Today

  • 24VDC power supply sizing starts with a full load list, counting PLC modules, transmitters at 22 mA, solenoid coils, relays and every other panel load.
  • Add 20 to 25 percent margin, then divide by the derating factor, which falls by 2.5 percent per kelvin above 60 °C for QUINT supplies.
  • Each redundant supply must carry the full load alone, and the voltage at the farthest field device must be checked with the load running.
